t: Lexicographically Smallest String After Operations With Constraint
o: Transform s into the lexicographically smallest t whose cyclic per-character distance from s totals at most k. Greedy works: scanning left to right, changing a character to 'a' costs d = min(c, 26−c) cyclic steps; spend budget whenever affordable since earlier positions dominate lexicographic order. If we cannot afford 'a' at a position, moving k steps downward (always possible when d > k, since then c > k) gives the smallest reachable character and exhausts the budget. Examples: "zbbz", k=3 → "aaaz"; "xaxcd", k=4 → "aawcd"; k=0 forces t = s.
k: Cyclic distance from c to 'a' is min(c, 26 − c); greedy left-to-right spending is optimal for lexicographic order.
If 'a' is unaffordable at a character c, then c > k, so shifting down by k is valid and yields the smallest feasible letter.
Budget never needs to be saved: later positions cannot compensate for a larger earlier character.

a.i: Walk the string once. At each character, if the cost to reach 'a' fits in the remaining budget, pay it; otherwise shift the character down by the entire remaining budget (legal because affordability failed implies c > k) and set the budget to zero.
s: For each character with value c: if min(c, 26−c) ≤ k, output 'a' and subtract the cost.
Else output chr(c − k + 'a') and set k = 0.

a.n: Approach 2: Per-position candidate scan with suffix feasibility
a.i: Precompute suffixMin[i] = minimum total cost to neutralize positions i..n−1 (each costs min(c, 26−c)). Then at each position try target letters 'a', 'b', … in order and take the first whose cyclic cost fits in the remaining budget minus the suffix minimum — a more mechanical way to see why the greedy choice is forced.
s: Compute suffixMin of per-character minimal distances.
For each position, iterate targets t = 0..25 in order.
Pick the first t with cyclicDist(c, t) ≤ remaining − suffixMin[i+1]; deduct its cost.
a.t: O(26 · n) — 26 candidate targets per position.
a.sp: O(n) for the suffix array and output.

w: Present the greedy; the suffix-feasibility version is a nice way to justify it if challenged. Pitfall: when 'a' is unaffordable, some try moving UP by k — that is only correct when moving down would underflow 'a', but unaffordability guarantees c > k so moving down is always legal and smaller. Edge cases: k = 0 returns s unchanged; k very large turns everything into "aaa…". Follow-up: maximize the string instead (greedy from the right), or a weighted per-position budget.
